items.stem: What is the main benefit of a protocol extension providing a default implementation?

options.text: Conforming types get shared behaviour without inheriting from a base class
options.rationale: Protocol extensions supply default methods, enabling protocol-oriented reuse.

options.text: It forces all conformers to be classes
options.rationale: Structs and enums can conform too.

options.text: It prevents the protocol from being adopted

items.explanation: Protocol extensions supply default methods, enabling protocol-oriented reuse.

items.stem: Select TWO ways to avoid a strong reference cycle when a closure captures self in Swift.

options.rationale: A weak capture does not keep self alive, breaking the cycle.

options.text: Capture self as unowned when self is guaranteed to outlive the closure
options.rationale: unowned avoids the cycle without optionality when lifetime is guaranteed.

options.text: Capture self strongly in an escaping closure
options.rationale: A strong capture in an escaping closure is what creates the cycle.

options.text: Mark the closure non-escaping and capture self strongly
options.rationale: The scenario in question involves escaping closures needing weak/unowned.

items.explanation: A weak capture does not keep self alive, breaking the cycle.

items.stem: Why does Swift distinguish escaping from non-escaping closures?

options.text: An escaping closure may be stored and run after the function returns, affecting memory
options.rationale: Escaping closures outlive the call, so capture and retain-cycle rules matter.

options.text: Escaping closures run on the main thread automatically

options.rationale: Non-escaping closures typically run synchronously within the call.

items.explanation: Escaping closures outlive the call, so capture and retain-cycle rules matter.
